## Step 6.1 · One variant by hand {#step-6-1}

We count cases and controls who carry at least one copy of a chosen DNA letter at one variant. We compare their odds of disease with those of non-carriers; odds are the number of cases divided by the number of controls. Then we fit the additive logistic model that the rest of the module uses, and connect its odds ratio to the carrier odds ratio.

[Read step 6.1 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-1).

```{r}
#| label: s6-1
report <- guided_path(cfg, "6.1", "example")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--snp", "9:96426973:A:G", "--export", "A", "--out", report))
x <- read.table(paste0(report, ".raw"), header = TRUE, check.names = FALSE)
dose <- as.numeric(x[[7]])  # <2>
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))
case <- psam$Disease[match(x$IID, psam$IID)] == "2"
tab <- table(case = case, carrier = dose > 0)  # <3>
print(tab)
carrier_or <- tab["TRUE", "TRUE"] * tab["FALSE", "FALSE"] / (tab["FALSE", "TRUE"] * tab["TRUE", "FALSE"])
print(c(counted_allele_column = names(x)[7], carrier_odds_ratio = carrier_or))
example <- data.frame(case = as.numeric(case), dosage = dose)  # <4>
fit <- glm(case ~ dosage, data = example, family = binomial())
print(summary(fit))  # <5>
print(exp(coef(fit)["dosage"]))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.1", paste0(report, ".raw"), parent = "5.7")
```

1. Export the number of copies of one DNA letter at the chosen variant.
2. Match the exported samples to their case or control status.
3. Count carriers and non-carriers and compare their odds of disease.
4. Fit the additive logistic model with the number of copies as the predictor.
5. Show the coefficients and the odds ratio per extra copy of the allele.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam, which hold the final study genotypes and sample details. |
| `--snp` | Selects only the variant named 9:96426973:A:G. |
| `--export` | Uses A format to write a .raw table with the number of copies of the named allele (DNA version) for each sample. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `A` | Writes one row per sample with allele copy counts of 0, 1 or 2, keeping missing values separate. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s6-1_example, including the s6-1_example.raw table. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

A table of carriers and non-carriers in the retained cohort, and a finite odds ratio. Read the direction of the odds ratio with the allele in the exported column. This allele is not always the one that raises risk. The model summary shows an intercept and a dosage coefficient, each with a standard error and a [p-value](#glossary-p-value). The odds ratio per copy and the carrier odds ratio need not be equal.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --snp 9:96426973:A:G --export A --out results/guided/s6-1_example --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

## Step 6.2 · Prepare covariates {#step-6-2}

We prepare covariates, extra factors used to adjust the disease comparison: age and ten numbers describing patterns of genetic variation. We match them to sample IDs and check for missing values and columns that repeat information from other columns.

[Read step 6.2 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-2).

```{r}
#| label: s6-2
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))  # <1>
pcs <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7", "pca"), ".eigenvec"))
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)
a <- match(psam$IID, metadata$IID); b <- match(psam$IID, pcs$IID)  # <2>
stopifnot(!anyNA(a), !anyNA(b), !anyDuplicated(pcs$IID))
covar <- data.frame(FID = psam$FID, IID = psam$IID, Age = as.numeric(metadata$Age[a]))
for (name in paste0("PC", 1:10)) covar[[name]] <- as.numeric(pcs[[name]][b])
stopifnot(!anyNA(covar))
design <- model.matrix(~ ., data = data.frame(SEX = as.numeric(psam$SEX), covar[, -(1:2)]))  # <3>
stopifnot(qr(design)$rank == ncol(design))
names(covar)[1] <- "#FID"
guided_write(covar, guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"))  # <4>
cat(nrow(covar), "complete covariate rows written\n")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.2", guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"), parent = "6.1")
```

1. Read sample details, genetic component scores and age records.
2. Match sample IDs and make a complete table of age and ten component scores.
3. Check that no model column repeats information from the other columns.
4. Save the covariate table and print its number of rows.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

1,811 complete covariate rows that match the samples, with Age and PC1 to PC10. There are no duplicate or unmatched IDs. The design has full column rank.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

:::

## Step 6.3 · Run the association scan {#step-6-3}

We test variants whose less common DNA version occurs at a frequency of at least 1% in the final study group. We adjust for age, sex and ten numbers describing genetic variation, then check and save the results.

[Read step 6.3 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-3).

```{r}
#| label: s6-3
out <- guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age,PC1-PC10", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", out))
results <- guided_association(out)
valid <- valid_p(results$P)  # <2>
stopifnot(sum(valid) == 236820L, sum(results$P[valid] < 5e-8) == 8L)
guided_write(results, guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "results.tsv"))  # <3>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.3", c(paste0(out, ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"), guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "results.tsv")), parent = "6.2")
```

1. Test variants with the frequency rule and the chosen adjustment factors.
2. Check the number of valid tests and results below the course significance threshold.
3. Save a table of the association results.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam, which hold the final study genotypes and sample details. |
| `--maf` | Keeps variants whose less common allele (DNA version) has a frequency of at least 1% in the final study group. |
| `--covar` | Reads s6-2_covariates.tsv, matching age and genetic component scores to samples by their IDs. |
| `--covar-name` | Selects Age and PC1 to PC10 as extra factors to adjust the disease comparison; each PC describes one pattern of genetic variation. |
| `--covar-variance-standardize` | Rescales the numerical adjustment factors to mean zero and variance one, a common scale that helps the model calculation remain stable. |
| `--glm` | Fits a logistic model at each variant to estimate how each extra copy of the tested DNA version changes the odds of disease. The odds of disease are the chance of having the disease divided by the chance of not having it. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sex` | Adds the recorded sex from s5-7_state.psam as an adjustment factor in the model. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `hide-covar` | Reports the genetic tests without separate rows for the effects of age, sex and genetic component scores. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `firth-fallback` | Uses Firth correction, which gives usable estimates when very few people carry the allele, when the ordinary model calculation fails. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s6-3_association, including s6-3_association.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

The frequency check in the final cohort removes another 1,693 variants. This leaves 236,820 additive p-values that are finite numbers. Eight of them are below 0.00000005. A variant kept before the scan can still fail the frequency check after the cohort changes. Read the output and the log. Never replace a missing result with zero.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --maf 0.01 --covar results/guided/s6-2_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age,PC1-PC10 --covar-variance-standardize --glm sex hide-covar firth-fallback --out results/guided/s6-3_association --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

## Step 6.4 · Read association output {#step-6-4}

We check model failure codes and calculate intervals that describe uncertainty in the estimated effects. We sort valid results by p-value, the chance of a result at least this extreme if the variant had no effect, and save the first 20 with their tested DNA letters and sample counts.

[Read step 6.4 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-4).

```{r}
#| label: s6-4
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"))  # <1>
print(table(results$ERRCODE, useNA = "ifany"))
valid <- results[valid_p(results$P), ]  # <2>
valid$CI_LOW <- exp(log(valid$OR) - 1.96 * valid[["LOG(OR)_SE"]])
valid$CI_HIGH <- exp(log(valid$OR) + 1.96 * valid[["LOG(OR)_SE"]])
top <- valid[order(valid$P), c("CHROM", "POS", "ID", "A1", "OBS_CT", "OR", "CI_LOW", "CI_HIGH", "P")]  # <3>
print(head(top, 10))
guided_write(head(top, 20), guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "top20.tsv"))  # <4>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.4", guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "top20.tsv"), parent = "6.3")
```

1. Read the scan results and count the model status codes.
2. Keep valid tests and calculate intervals describing uncertainty in their effects.
3. Sort by p-value and print the first ten results with their tested DNA letters.
4. Save the first 20 results for later review.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

The leading regions are on chromosomes 9, 3 and 12. The table keeps the effect allele and the OBS_CT of each variant. Every p-value and odds ratio refers to the tested A1 allele, whatever the variant ID looks like.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

:::

## Step 6.5 · Sparse genotypes and Firth correction {#step-6-5}

We choose the variant with the lowest frequency of its less common DNA version among the valid tests on chromosomes 1 to 22 and compare its ordinary model result with a forced Firth result. Firth correction gives usable estimates when very few people carry the allele, but it does not add information.

[Read step 6.5 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-5).

```{r}
#| label: s6-5
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"))  # <1>
minor <- pmin(results$A1_FREQ, 1 - results$A1_FREQ)
candidates <- which(results$CHROM %in% as.character(1:22) & valid_p(results$P) & minor > 0)
chosen <- results$ID[candidates[which.min(minor[candidates])]]
guided_list(chosen, guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "variant.txt"))  # <2>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--snp", chosen, "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age,PC1-PC10", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "firth", "sex", "hide-covar", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "firth")))
comparison <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.5", "firth"))  # <3>
print(results[results$ID == chosen, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
print(comparison[, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
stopifnot(nrow(comparison) == 1L, valid_p(comparison$P))
```

1. Choose the least frequent variant among valid tests on chromosomes 1 to 22.
2. Save the chosen variant ID and force the Firth model at that variant.
3. Print both estimates and check that the Firth test gives one valid result.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, .pvar and .psam, which hold the final study genotypes and sample details. |
| `--snp` | Selects the one variant that R chose from the valid tests on chromosomes 1 to 22: the variant with the lowest frequency of its less common DNA version. R saves its ID in s6-5_variant.txt. In a terminal, type that ID instead of VARIANT_ID. |
| `--covar` | Reads s6-2_covariates.tsv, matching age and genetic component scores to samples by their IDs. |
| `--covar-name` | Selects Age and PC1 to PC10 as extra factors to adjust the disease comparison; each PC describes one pattern of genetic variation. |
| `--covar-variance-standardize` | Rescales the numerical adjustment factors to mean zero and variance one, a common scale that helps the model calculation remain stable. |
| `--glm` | Fits a logistic model at the selected variant to estimate how each extra copy of the tested DNA version changes the odds of disease. The odds of disease are the chance of having the disease divided by the chance of not having it. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `firth` | Always uses Firth correction, which gives usable estimates when very few people carry the allele, rather than waiting for the ordinary model calculation to fail. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sex` | Adds the recorded sex from s5-7_state.psam as an adjustment factor in the model. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `hide-covar` | Reports the genetic test without separate rows for the effects of age, sex and genetic component scores. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s6-5_firth for the forced Firth result. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

One forced Firth result with a finite value, next to the ordinary estimate from the main scan for the same A1 allele. Small differences in the numbers are normal. Forced Firth is not a better scan for the whole genome.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --snp VARIANT_ID --covar results/guided/s6-2_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age,PC1-PC10 --covar-variance-standardize --glm firth sex hide-covar --out results/guided/s6-5_firth --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

## Step 6.6 · First look and association checkpoint {#step-6-6}

We summarise the sample and variant counts, valid tests and results below the course significance threshold of 5 × 10⁻⁸ (0.00000005). We also measure whether test values are generally larger than expected without effects and save the key files in a checked checkpoint for restarting.

[Read step 6.6 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-6).

```{r}
#| label: s6-6
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"))  # <1>
summary <- data.frame(samples = 1811, retained_variants = 238513, finite_tests = sum(valid_p(results$P)),
  genome_wide = sum(results$P[valid_p(results$P)] < 5e-8),
  lambda_autosomes = lambda_gc(results$P[results$CHROM %in% as.character(1:22)]))
guided_write(summary, guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "summary.tsv"))  # <2>
print(summary)
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
files <- c(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"), ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"),
  guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"), guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "top20.tsv"), guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "summary.tsv"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.6", files)
check_step("6.6", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

1. Read the results and summarise the study size and test values.
2. Save and print the summary table.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

1,811 retained samples, 238,513 retained variants and 236,820 tests with finite p-values. Eight variants are genome-wide significant. The autosomal [lambda](#glossary-lambda-gc) is about 1.016. The key analysis files get a manifest: a list of files with their [SHA-256](#glossary-sha-256) checksums.

## Step 6.7 · Create the summary statistics file {#step-6-7}

We save the scan results in a standard table with one row per tested variant and a separate file explaining its columns. We read the saved table back and check its values and counts so the next plots use a verified file.

[Read step 6.7 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-6/step-6-7).

```{r}
#| label: s6-7
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"))  # <1>
stats <- guided_standardise_scan(results)
guided_check_summary(stats, rows = nrow(results))  # <2>
stats_file <- guided_summary_path(cfg)
guided_write_summary(stats, stats_file)  # <3>
dictionary_file <- guided_path(cfg, "6.7", "gwas_summary_statistics_columns.tsv")
guided_write(guided_summary_dictionary(), dictionary_file)
# Read the file back, as the plots will, and check that nothing was lost.
saved <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <4>
guided_check_summary(saved, rows = nrow(results))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(saved, stats)))
first_summary <- read.delim(guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "summary.tsv"))  # <5>
finite <- valid_p(saved$p_value)
stopifnot(sum(finite) == first_summary$finite_tests, sum(saved$p_value[finite] < 5e-8) == first_summary$genome_wide)
print(head(saved, 5))
print(c(rows = nrow(saved), finite_tests = sum(finite), missing_p_values = sum(is.na(saved$p_value)),
  genome_wide = sum(saved$p_value[finite] < 5e-8)))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "6.7", c(stats_file, dictionary_file), parent = "6.6")
check_step("6.7", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
```

1. Read the scan and arrange its results in the standard columns.
2. Check the columns and values and choose the summary file name.
3. Save the summary table and a file explaining each column.
4. Read the saved table and check that it matches the original results.
5. Compare test counts with the saved scan summary and print the checked results.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

The summary statistics file has 236,820 rows, one for each tested variant. It has the eleven columns in the order of the table above. The checks stop the step with an error if a column name, a p-value or an odds ratio breaks the rules. The first row is `1:858952:G:A`, with effect allele `A`, other allele `G`, odds ratio 1.03471, `beta` about 0.034 and n = 1807. `beta` is calculated from the odds ratio that PLINK writes, so it is the logarithm of that rounded value. No p-value is missing in this dataset. Eight p-values are below 0.00000005, as at 6.6. The file is about 22 MB. The column file has one row for each of the eleven columns. The last table shows `matches` for both files in the 6.7 checkpoint.

If PLINK could not calculate a p-value, the file would show `NA`. It would never show 0 or 1.

:::

## Step 7.1 · QQ plot {#step-7-1}

We draw a QQ plot, which compares observed p-values with those expected by chance, using chromosomes 1 to 22. This helps us see whether most tests behave as expected and whether the results with the smallest p-values stand out.

[Read step 7.1 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-1).

```{r}
#| label: s7-1
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <1>
autosomal <- stats$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)  # <2>
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.1", "qq.png"), function() plot_qq(stats$p_value[autosomal], "Adjusted simulated GWAS: autosomal QQ plot"))  # <3>
```

1. Read the saved association summary table.
2. Select chromosomes 1 to 22 for the plot.
3. Save the plot comparing observed p-values with values expected by chance.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Most points are close to the diagonal line. The highest points at the right end leave the line by a wide margin. Missing, zero or invalid p-values are not drawn as if they were very small p-values. R saves the picture as a PNG file and prints its path. It does not show the picture in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

:::

## Step 7.2 · Genomic inflation factor {#step-7-2}

We calculate lambda, a number that compares the middle of the test results with what chance predicts. We check that it is close to 1.016 and save it to help assess the results alongside the QQ plot.

[Read step 7.2 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-2).

```{r}
#| label: s7-2
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <1>
p <- stats$p_value[stats$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)]  # <2>
lambda <- lambda_gc(p)  # <3>
print(lambda)
stopifnot(abs(lambda - 1.016) < 0.001)
guided_write(data.frame(model = "QC plus ten PCs", lambda = lambda), guided_path(cfg, "7.2", "lambda.tsv"))  # <4>
```

1. Read the saved association summary table.
2. Select p-values for chromosomes 1 to 22.
3. Calculate and check the overall size of the test results.
4. Save lambda in a table.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Lambda is approximately 1.016. R calculates it from the valid autosomal tests.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

## Step 7.3 · Manhattan plot {#step-7-3}

We draw a Manhattan plot, which shows the strength of each result at its position along chromosomes 1 to 22, and label the lead variant of each region. We also check that eight variants have p-values below 5 × 10⁻⁸ (0.00000005) to confirm the count of results with very small p-values.

[Read step 7.3 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-3).

```{r}
#| label: s7-3
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <1>
plot_data <- data.frame(CHROM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(stats$chromosome)),  # <2>
  POS = stats$base_pair_location, P = stats$p_value)
leads <- region_leads(plot_data$CHROM, plot_data$POS, plot_data$P)  # <3>
plot_data$LABEL <- NA_character_
plot_data$LABEL[leads$index] <- guided_variant_labels(cfg, leads$chromosome, leads$position, stats$variant_id[leads$index])
# Optional: suggestive = TRUE adds a dotted line at 5e-5. label_leads = FALSE hides the rs numbers.
# max_labels sets how many regions get a label (the regions with the smallest p-values come first).
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan.png"), function() plot_manhattan(plot_data, "Simulated GWAS: age, sex and ten PCs",  # <4>
  suggestive = FALSE, label_leads = TRUE, max_labels = 3))
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan_suggestive.png"), function() plot_manhattan(plot_data, "Simulated GWAS: age, sex and ten PCs",  # <5>
  suggestive = TRUE, label_leads = TRUE, max_labels = 3))
stopifnot(sum(stats$p_value[valid_p(stats$p_value)] < 5e-8) == 8L)  # <6>
```

1. Read the saved association summary table.
2. Prepare the chromosome, position and p-value columns.
3. Find the lead variant of each region below 5e-8 and look up its rs number.
4. Save the plot of results along the chromosomes.
5. Save a second picture with the optional suggestive line switched on.
6. Check that eight variants have p-values below 0.00000005.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

There are three regions with very small p-values, on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12. Together they hold eight variants below 5e-8. The lead variants carry the labels rs1994750 on chromosome 3, rs10820598 on chromosome 9 and rs7953249 on chromosome 12. The moderate region that we planted does not reach this usual threshold. Tests on the sex chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA (MT) stay in the result table, but this figure shows only the autosomes. R saves two pictures as PNG files and prints the path of each one. The second picture is the same plot with the dotted suggestive line at 5e-5 switched on. It does not show the pictures in the console. To see it, open the file from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

:::

## Step 7.4 · Multiple-testing thresholds {#step-7-4}

We compare three rules for multiple testing, which means allowing for the many chances to obtain a false result. We count p-values below 5 × 10⁻⁸ (0.00000005), p-values below 0.05 divided by the number of valid tests, and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values below 0.05. The third rule controls the expected share of false results among those called significant.

[Read step 7.4 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-4).

```{r}
#| label: s7-4
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <1>
p <- stats$p_value[valid_p(stats$p_value)]  # <2>
threshold <- data.frame(rule = c("Conventional GWAS", "Bonferroni for this scan", "BH adjusted p at 0.05"),  # <3>
  threshold = c(5e-8, 0.05 / length(p), 0.05),
  discoveries = c(sum(p < 5e-8), sum(p < 0.05 / length(p)), sum(p.adjust(p, method = "BH") < 0.05)))
print(threshold)
guided_write(threshold, guided_path(cfg, "7.4", "thresholds.tsv"))  # <4>
```

1. Read the saved association summary table.
2. Keep only valid p-values.
3. Compare three rules for deciding which results are convincing enough.
4. Save the threshold comparison table.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

There are 236,820 finite tests, so the Bonferroni threshold for this scan is approximately 2.11e-7. The usual threshold gives eight discoveries. BH answers a different question about errors, so it can return more.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

No PLINK equivalent

:::

## Step 7.5 · Clump correlated results {#step-7-5}

We group nearby variants whose DNA patterns are correlated, meaning they tend to vary together across people. We use the final cohort to measure this similarity and check that the significant results form three groups.

[Read step 7.5 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-5).

```{r}
#| label: s7-5
report <- guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--clump", paste0(guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "association"), ".Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid"),  # <2>
  "--clump-id-field", "ID", "--clump-p-field", "P", "--clump-p1", "5e-8", "--clump-p2", "1e-5",
  "--clump-r2", "0.1", "--clump-kb", "250", "--clump-unphased", "--out", report))
clumps <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".clumps"))  # <3>
print(clumps)
stopifnot(nrow(clumps) == 3L)
```

1. Choose the name for the grouped association results.
2. Group nearby correlated variants using the final cohort.
3. Read the groups and check that there are three.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, s5-7_state.pvar and s5-7_state.psam, which hold the final cohort's DNA calls, variant information and sample information. |
| `--clump` | Reads s6-3_association.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid and groups nearby association results whose DNA patterns are correlated across samples. |
| `--clump-id-field` | Uses the ID column of the association report to identify variants. |
| `--clump-p-field` | Uses the P column of the association report for p-values, which measure how unusual each result would be without an effect. |
| `--clump-p1` | Allows a variant to lead a group when its p-value is at most 5 × 10⁻⁸ (0.00000005). |
| `--clump-p2` | Lists other variants in a group when their p-values are at most 1 × 10⁻⁵ (0.00001). |
| `--clump-r2` | Adds variants whose squared correlation with the group's lead variant exceeds 0.1. |
| `--clump-kb` | Limits each group to variants within 250 kilobases, or 250,000 DNA positions, on either side of its lead variant. |
| `--clump-unphased` | Calculates correlation from the number of copies of a DNA version at each variant, without assigning those copies to individual chromosomes. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-5_clump, including the grouped results in s7-5_clump.clumps. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

There are three clumps. They describe the regions with very small p-values on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12. The report gives the ID and the p-value of each lead variant. This does not show that there are three causal variants.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --clump results/guided/s6-3_association.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid --clump-id-field ID --clump-p-field P --clump-p1 5e-8 --clump-p2 1e-5 --clump-r2 0.1 --clump-kb 250 --clump-unphased --out results/guided/s7-5_clump --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

## Step 7.6 · Regional plot {#step-7-6}

We draw three detailed regional plots, one for each region with genome-wide significant variants, on chromosomes 3, 9 and 12. Each plot shows the strength of each association and how closely its DNA pattern follows the lead variant, using a continuous colour scale.

[Read step 7.6 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-6).

```{r}
#| label: s7-6
regions <- data.frame(label = c("L1", "L2", "L3"), chromosome = c("3", "9", "12"),  # <1>
  position = c(163224115, 96426973, 120965921), lead = c("3:163224115:T:C", "9:96426973:A:G", "12:120965921:G:A"),
  ld = c("ld_chr3", "ld", "ld_chr12"), picture = c("regional_chr3.png", "regional.png", "regional_chr12.png"),
  expected = c(1L, 4L, 3L), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <2>
regions$rs <- guided_variant_labels(cfg, regions$chromosome, regions$position, regions$lead)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(regions))) {  # <3>
  report <- guided_path(cfg, "7.6", regions$ld[i])
  run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--chr", regions$chromosome[i],
    "--from-bp", format(regions$position[i] - 500000, scientific = FALSE), "--to-bp", format(regions$position[i] + 500000, scientific = FALSE),
    "--r2-unphased", "--ld-snp", regions$lead[i], "--ld-window-kb", "500", "--ld-window-r2", "0", "--out", report))
  ld <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".vcor"))  # <4>
  region <- stats[stats$chromosome == regions$chromosome[i] & abs(stats$base_pair_location - regions$position[i]) <= 500000 & valid_p(stats$p_value), ]
  r2_column <- grep("R2$", names(ld), value = TRUE)  # <5>
  stopifnot(length(r2_column) == 1L)
  r2 <- as.numeric(ld[[r2_column]][match(region$variant_id, ld$ID_B)])  # <6>
  r2[region$variant_id == regions$lead[i]] <- 1
  png(guided_path(cfg, "7.6", regions$picture[i]), width = 1500, height = 900, res = 150)  # <7>
  plot_regional(region, r2, match(regions$lead[i], region$variant_id), regions$chromosome[i], regions$rs[i],
    paste0(regions$label[i], ": association and LD to the lead"))
  invisible(dev.off())
  cat("The plot was saved to ", guided_path(cfg, "7.6", regions$picture[i]), "\n", sep = "")
  stopifnot(sum(region$p_value < 5e-8) == regions$expected[i])  # <8>
}
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "7.6", c(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "ld"), ".vcor"), guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png")), parent = "6.7")
```

1. List the three regions, their lead variants, output names and the expected number of genome-wide significant variants.
2. Read the association results once and look up the rs number of each lead variant.
3. For each region, measure correlations with the lead within 500,000 DNA positions and draw the plot.
4. Read the correlation table and select the regional association results.
5. Find and check the column holding squared correlations.
6. Match each regional variant to its correlation with the lead variant.
7. Draw and save the regional plot with a continuous colour scale, the lead label and the significance line.
8. Check the number of regional variants with p-values below 0.00000005.

### What each option does

**Command 1: measure correlation around the chromosome 3 lead**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, s5-7_state.pvar and s5-7_state.psam, which hold the final cohort's DNA calls, variant information and sample information. |
| `--chr` | Selects chromosome 3 for the regional comparison. |
| `--from-bp` | Starts the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 162724115. |
| `--to-bp` | Ends the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 163724115. |
| `--r2-unphased` | Reports squared correlations between the numbers of copies of DNA versions at pairs of variants, without assigning copies to individual chromosomes. |
| `--ld-snp` | Pairs variant 3:163224115:T:C with the other selected variants to measure their correlation with it. |
| `--ld-window-kb` | Limits pairs to variants within 500 kilobases, or 500,000 DNA positions, of variant 3:163224115:T:C. |
| `--ld-window-r2` | Sets the minimum reported squared correlation to 0 so weak correlations remain in the report. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-6_ld_chr3, including the correlation table s7-6_ld_chr3.vcor. |

**Command 2: measure correlation around the chromosome 9 lead**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, s5-7_state.pvar and s5-7_state.psam, which hold the final cohort's DNA calls, variant information and sample information. |
| `--chr` | Selects chromosome 9 for the regional comparison. |
| `--from-bp` | Starts the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 95926973. |
| `--to-bp` | Ends the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 96926973. |
| `--r2-unphased` | Reports squared correlations between the numbers of copies of DNA versions at pairs of variants, without assigning copies to individual chromosomes. |
| `--ld-snp` | Pairs variant 9:96426973:A:G with the other selected variants to measure their correlation with it. |
| `--ld-window-kb` | Limits pairs to variants within 500 kilobases, or 500,000 DNA positions, of variant 9:96426973:A:G. |
| `--ld-window-r2` | Sets the minimum reported squared correlation to 0 so weak correlations remain in the report. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-6_ld, including the correlation table s7-6_ld.vcor. |

**Command 3: measure correlation around the chromosome 12 lead**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, s5-7_state.pvar and s5-7_state.psam, which hold the final cohort's DNA calls, variant information and sample information. |
| `--chr` | Selects chromosome 12 for the regional comparison. |
| `--from-bp` | Starts the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 120465921. |
| `--to-bp` | Ends the selected GRCh38 interval at DNA position 121465921. |
| `--r2-unphased` | Reports squared correlations between the numbers of copies of DNA versions at pairs of variants, without assigning copies to individual chromosomes. |
| `--ld-snp` | Pairs variant 12:120965921:G:A with the other selected variants to measure their correlation with it. |
| `--ld-window-kb` | Limits pairs to variants within 500 kilobases, or 500,000 DNA positions, of variant 12:120965921:G:A. |
| `--ld-window-r2` | Sets the minimum reported squared correlation to 0 so weak correlations remain in the report. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-6_ld_chr12, including the correlation table s7-6_ld_chr12.vcor. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

L2 has four genome-wide significant variants. L1 has one and L3 has three. Together they are the eight variants that we found at step 7.3. Each plot shows LD as a continuous colour from pale yellow (r^2 of 0) to dark purple (r^2 of 1). The lead variant is a labelled black diamond: rs1994750 for L1, rs10820598 for L2 and rs7953249 for L3. If an LD value is missing, the legend says "LD unavailable". The value is not silently set to zero. R saves three pictures as PNG files and prints the path of each one. It does not show the pictures in the console. To see them, open the files from the Files pane of RStudio (click the file name, then choose "View File").

::: {.callout-tip title="Another approach (optional)" collapse="true"}

This box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it. It reads the association results only and writes nothing to disk.

A lead variant is the variant with the smallest p-value in a region. It is not always the causal variant, because nearby variants are correlated. Fine-mapping asks which variants could be causal. A 95% credible set is a group of variants that holds the causal variant with a probability of 95%, under the assumptions of the method. The set is not a list of certain causes.

The method here is Wakefield's approximate Bayes factor (ABF). For each variant, it uses the estimate of the effect (the log odds ratio) and its standard error. It compares two ideas: this variant has an effect, or it has none. The effect under the first idea comes from a prior. The prior is a normal distribution with mean 0 and a standard deviation of 0.2 on the log odds ratio. Its variance W is 0.04. This means that most true effects are small, and an odds ratio of about 1.5 (log 0.4, two standard deviations) is already large. The Bayes factors of all variants in a region are then scaled to add up to 1. Each scaled value is the posterior inclusion probability (PIP) of the variant. We add the variants from the highest PIP down until the sum reaches 95%.

There is one important limit. The method assumes that the region holds exactly one causal variant. If a region has two or more, the PIPs are not valid. The method SuSiE removes this limit, because it can fit several causal variants in one region (Wang et al. 2020, [doi:10.1111/rssb.12388](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12388)). We do not run it here.

```{r}
#| label: s7-6_credible_sets
#| eval: false
# Optional. This reads the objects `regions` and `stats` made in the chunk of this step. It writes no file.
credible <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(regions)), function(i) {  # <1>
  region <- stats[stats$chromosome == regions$chromosome[i] & abs(stats$base_pair_location - regions$position[i]) <= 500000 & valid_p(stats$p_value), ]
  c(list(variants = nrow(region)), credible_set(region$variant_id, region$beta, region$standard_error, prior_sd = 0.2, level = 0.95))  # <2>
})
data.frame(region = regions$label, lead = regions$rs, variants_in_region = sapply(credible, function(x) x$variants),  # <3>
           set_size = sapply(credible, function(x) x$size), lead_pip = round(sapply(credible, function(x) x$lead_pip), 3))
```

1. For each region, take the variants within 500,000 DNA positions of the lead variant.
2. Calculate the credible set with a prior standard deviation of 0.2 on the log odds ratio (W = 0.04).
3. Show one row for each region: the size of the set and the PIP of the lead variant.


Plain PLINK 2 command: not applicable. R calculates the Bayes factors from the summary statistics.

Expected result.

| Region | Lead variant | Variants in the region | Variants in the 95% set | PIP of the lead variant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L1 (chromosome 3) | rs1994750 | 42 | 1 | 1.000 |
| L2 (chromosome 9) | rs10820598 | 66 | 1 | 0.994 |
| L3 (chromosome 12) | rs7953249 | 94 | 2 | 0.918 |

How to read it. In L1 and L2 the set holds only the lead variant. The lead variant has a much smaller p-value than its neighbours, so the method gives it almost all the probability. In L3 the set holds two variants, and the lead variant has a PIP of 0.918. A small set does not prove that the variant is causal. It depends on the prior, on the single-variant assumption and on the variants that the array measured. The causal variant may not be on the array at all. Do not read the set as a gene or a mechanism. The data are simulated, so the loci carry no biology.

References. The approximate Bayes factor: Wakefield 2009, [doi:10.1002/gepi.20359](https://doi.org/10.1002/gepi.20359). Credible sets from Bayes factors in a region: Maller et al. 2012, [doi:10.1038/ng.2435](https://doi.org/10.1038/ng.2435). SuSiE: Wang et al. 2020, [doi:10.1111/rssb.12388](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12388).

:::

## Step 7.7 · Compare without PCs and without QC {#step-7-7}

We repeat the association tests without genetic components, the numbers that summarise ancestry, and then without sample and variant quality checks as well. We compare counts and plots to see how these choices change the results.

[Read step 7.7 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-7).

```{r}
#| label: s7-7
no_pc <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "no_pcs")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.2", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", no_pc))
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)  # <2>
all_covar <- metadata[c("FID", "IID", "Age")]; names(all_covar)[1] <- "#FID"
all_file <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "all_ages.tsv"); guided_write(all_covar, all_file)
no_qc <- guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "no_qc_no_pcs")  # <3>
baseline <- guided_path(cfg, "2.8")
if (!file.exists(paste0(baseline, ".pgen"))) baseline <- file.path(cfg$data_dir, "checkpoints", "2.8", "state")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", baseline, "--maf", "0.01", "--covar", all_file,  # <4>
  "--covar-name", "Age", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "sex", "hide-covar", "firth-fallback", "--out", no_qc))
main <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)  # <5>
a <- guided_standardise_scan(guided_association(no_pc))
b <- guided_standardise_scan(guided_association(no_qc))
k <- match(main$variant_id, a$variant_id)  # <6>
stopifnot(!anyNA(k), all(main$n == a$n[k]))
autosomal_p <- function(x) x$p_value[x$chromosome %in% as.character(1:22)]  # <7>
summarise <- function(x) c(finite_tests = sum(valid_p(x$p_value)), hits = sum(x$p_value[valid_p(x$p_value)] < 5e-8),
  lambda = lambda_gc(autosomal_p(x)))
comparison <- rbind(main = summarise(main), no_PCs = summarise(a), no_sample_or_variant_QC_no_PCs = summarise(b))
print(comparison)
stopifnot(comparison[2, "hits"] == 17L, comparison[3, "hits"] == 19L)
guided_write(data.frame(model = rownames(comparison), comparison, row.names = NULL), guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"))  # <8>
# The order goes from the least adjusted analysis to the most adjusted one.
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "qq_comparison.png"), function() {  # <9>
  par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
  plotted <- list(autosomal_p(b), autosomal_p(a), autosomal_p(main))
  limits <- c(0, max(-log10(unlist(plotted))))
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(b), "No sample/variant QC, no PCs", ylim = limits)
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(a), "QC, no PCs", ylim = limits)
  plot_qq(autosomal_p(main), "QC + ten PCs", ylim = limits)
}, width = 2100, height = 750)
manhattan_data <- function(x) {  # <10>
  d <- data.frame(CHROM = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x$chromosome)), POS = x$base_pair_location, P = x$p_value, LABEL = NA_character_)
  leads <- region_leads(d$CHROM, d$POS, d$P)
  d$LABEL[leads$index] <- guided_variant_labels(cfg, leads$chromosome, leads$position, x$variant_id[leads$index])
  d
}
panels <- list(b = manhattan_data(b), a = manhattan_data(a), main = manhattan_data(main))
top <- max(8, -log10(unlist(lapply(panels, function(d) d$P[valid_p(d$P)]))))  # <11>
# Optional: suggestive = TRUE adds the dotted line at 5e-5 to every panel. max_labels sets how many regions get a label.
save_plot(guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "manhattan_comparison.png"), function() {  # <12>
  par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(4, 4.5, 3, 1))
  plot_manhattan(panels$b, "No sample/variant QC, no PCs", suggestive = FALSE, label_leads = TRUE, max_labels = 5, ylim = c(0, top))
  plot_manhattan(panels$a, "QC, no PCs", suggestive = FALSE, label_leads = TRUE, max_labels = 5, ylim = c(0, top))
  plot_manhattan(panels$main, "QC + ten PCs", suggestive = FALSE, label_leads = TRUE, max_labels = 5, ylim = c(0, top))
}, width = 1800, height = 2400)
```

1. Repeat the final cohort analysis using age and sex without genetic components.
2. Read the original sample information and save ages for all wells.
3. Choose the output name and find the cohort saved before quality checks.
4. Test the cohort before sample and variant quality checks using age and sex.
5. Read the main results and put the comparison results into matching columns.
6. Check that the main and cleaned comparison analyses use the same samples per variant.
7. Count valid tests and results below the genome-wide threshold and calculate lambda for each analysis.
8. Save the comparison table.
9. Save three QQ plots with the same scale to compare the analyses.
10. Prepare the same three analyses for Manhattan plots. Each lead variant gets its rs number as a label.
11. Use one vertical scale for all three Manhattan plots, so that the heights can be compared.
12. Save the Manhattan comparison, again from the least to the most adjusted analysis.

### What each option does

**Command 1: test the final cohort without genetic components**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads s5-7_state.pgen, s5-7_state.pvar and s5-7_state.psam, which hold the final cohort's DNA calls, variant information and sample information. |
| `--maf` | Tests only variants whose less common DNA version has a frequency of at least 0.01, or 1%, in the input cohort. |
| `--covar` | Reads s6-2_covariates.tsv and matches adjustment values to samples by their identifiers. |
| `--covar-name` | Selects only Age from the adjustment table, leaving out genetic component scores that summarise ancestry. |
| `--covar-variance-standardize` | Rescales age to have a mean of zero and a variance of one so the model calculation remains stable. |
| `--glm` | Fits a logistic model at each variant to estimate how each extra copy of the tested DNA version changes the odds of disease. The odds of disease are the chance of having the disease divided by the chance of not having it. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sex` | Adds recorded sex from the input sample file as an adjustment factor. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `hide-covar` | Reports genetic tests without separate rows for the effects of age and sex. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `firth-fallback` | Uses Firth correction, which gives usable estimates when very few people carry the allele, when the ordinary model calculation fails. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-7_no_pcs, including s7-7_no_pcs.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid. |

**Command 2: test the cohort before sample and variant quality checks**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the cohort before sample and variant quality checks from s2-8_state.pgen, s2-8_state.pvar and s2-8_state.psam. If the local PGEN file is absent, R uses checkpoints/2.8/state in the course data folder. |
| `--maf` | Tests only variants whose less common DNA version has a frequency of at least 0.01, or 1%, in the input cohort. |
| `--covar` | Reads s7-7_all_ages.tsv, which holds ages for all measured wells, and matches them to samples by their identifiers. |
| `--covar-name` | Selects only Age from the adjustment table, leaving out genetic component scores that summarise ancestry. |
| `--covar-variance-standardize` | Rescales age to have a mean of zero and a variance of one so the model calculation remains stable. |
| `--glm` | Fits a logistic model at each variant to estimate how each extra copy of the tested DNA version changes the odds of disease. The odds of disease are the chance of having the disease divided by the chance of not having it. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sex` | Adds recorded sex from the input sample file as an adjustment factor. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `hide-covar` | Reports genetic tests without separate rows for the effects of age and sex. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `firth-fallback` | Uses Firth correction, which gives usable estimates when very few people carry the allele, when the ordinary model calculation fails. |
| `--out` | Starts output file names with s7-7_no_qc_no_pcs, including s7-7_no_qc_no_pcs.Disease.glm.logistic.hybrid. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Main analysis: 236,820 tests, eight hits, lambda about 1.016. Without PCs after QC: 236,820 tests, 17 hits, lambda about 1.527. Without sample or variant QC and without PCs: 239,647 tests, 19 hits, lambda about 1.655. The extra peaks do not show that worse QC finds more true causes.

The plots follow the order from the least adjusted analysis to the most adjusted one. All QQ plots share one vertical scale. All three Manhattan plots also share one vertical scale, so you can compare the heights of the peaks. Each plot has the genome-wide line at 5e-8, and the labels show the rs number of the lead variant of each region. The table below summarises the same numbers in that order.

| Analysis | Hits below 5e-8 | Lambda |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No sample or variant QC, no PCs | 19 | about 1.655 |
| QC, no PCs | 17 | about 1.527 |
| QC and ten PCs (main analysis) | 8 | about 1.016 |

Without PCs, the same three peaks stay and some points reach a little higher. Without any QC, the plot also shows peaks on chromosomes 2 and 15 just above the line, and the lead variant on chromosome 12 changes to rs7310409. The label exm2265352 is an array name, because that variant has no rs number. A lead variant that appears only in the weaker analyses is a warning sign, not a discovery.

:::

## Step 7.8 · Final summary and reporting {#step-7-8}

We save a final report and a table of the lead variant in each of the three groups. We calculate intervals that describe uncertainty in the estimated effects and check the saved report, tables and main figures so others can review the analysis.

[Read step 7.8 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-7/step-7-8).

```{r}
#| label: s7-8
psam <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), ".psam"))  # <1>
comparison <- read.delim(guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"))
clumps <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump"), ".clumps"))
stats <- guided_summary_stats(cfg)
lead <- stats[match(clumps$ID, stats$variant_id), c("chromosome", "base_pair_location", "variant_id", "effect_allele", "odds_ratio", "beta", "standard_error", "p_value", "n")]  # <2>
lead$ci_low <- exp(lead$beta - 1.96 * lead$standard_error)
lead$ci_high <- exp(lead$beta + 1.96 * lead$standard_error)
guided_write(lead, guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "leads.tsv"))  # <3>
summary <- c("# Simulated GWAS: main-path summary", "", "Genome assembly: GRCh38. Simulated data, seed 20261111.",  # <4>
  paste("Software:", paste(cfg$version, collapse = "; ")),
  "Initial: 2,016 measured wells, 2,000 people, 299,523 variant entries.",
  paste("Final cohort:", nrow(psam), "samples; cases:", sum(psam$Disease == "2"), "; controls:", sum(psam$Disease == "1")),
  "After QC: 238,513 variants; 236,820 finite additive association tests.",
  "Model: additive logistic regression, adjusted for age, recorded sex and ten within-cohort PCs; Firth fallback enabled.",
  "Eight variants pass p < 5e-8 in three LD clumps. Autosomal lambda is approximately 1.016.",
  "Report the effect allele, odds ratio, 95% interval, p-value and per-variant sample count n from s7-8_leads.tsv.",
  "Interpretation: the three simulated regions with very small p-values are recovered; the moderate region is subthreshold. No causal gene is established.",
  "Sensitivity: omitting PCs increases lambda to approximately 1.546; omitting sample/variant QC as well gives approximately 1.655.",
  "Limitations: simulated design, selected array sites, finite power, provisional imported REF labels, study-specific QC and ancestry rules.",
  "Three named ancestry markers left at HWE step 4.4; comparisons must not pretend they survived to module 5.",
  "Figures: s7-1_qq.png, s7-3_manhattan.png, s7-6_regional.png and s7-7_qq_comparison.png.",
  "No biological discovery or clinical recommendation follows from this simulation.")
writeLines(summary, guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "summary.md"), useBytes = TRUE)  # <5>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
files <- c(guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "summary.md"), guided_path(cfg, "7.8", "leads.tsv"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.1", "qq.png"), guided_path(cfg, "7.3", "manhattan.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.6", "regional.png"), guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "qq_comparison.png"),
  guided_path(cfg, "7.7", "comparison.tsv"), paste0(guided_path(cfg, "7.5", "clump"), ".clumps"),
  file.path(cfg$out, "step_counts.tsv"), file.path(cfg$out, "software_versions.txt"))
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "7.8", files, parent = "6.7")
check_step("7.8", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)
cat(paste(summary, collapse = "\n"), "\n")  # <6>
```

1. Read the final sample counts, comparison table, variant groups and association results.
2. Select the lead variant in each group and calculate its uncertainty interval.
3. Save the table of the three lead variants.
4. Prepare the report describing the analysis, results and limitations.
5. Save the report as a text file.
6. Print the final report.

# Glossary terms used in this notebook {#glossary}

These entries repeat the course glossary so that every link in this notebook works offline.

## FID / IID {#glossary-fid-iid .unlisted}

The identifier pair used to match samples between files.

## GRCh38 {#glossary-grch38 .unlisted}

The 2013 version of the human reference genome. Each position in the genome has a coordinate in this version, and files must use the same version to be compared.

## Lambda GC {#glossary-lambda-gc .unlisted}

Summary of test-statistic inflation/deflation, not proof of a valid model.

## p-value {#glossary-p-value .unlisted}

Under the null model, probability of a statistic at least as extreme as observed.

## Plus strand {#glossary-plus-strand .unlisted}

One of the two strands of the DNA double helix, used as the common reference for writing alleles. Using the plus strand for all sites avoids confusion between the two strands.

## Reference allele {#glossary-reference-allele .unlisted}

The allele that matches the reference genome at a site. It is often written REF. The other allele is often written ALT.

## SHA-256 {#glossary-sha-256 .unlisted}

A short code calculated from the content of a file. If the file changes, the code changes, so it shows whether a file is intact.
